After careful review of the Home Health Grouping Model (HHGM) proposal, the methodology of implementation is contrary to center of Medicare and Medicaid practices. 

When PPS was introduced in 1999, it was met with anxiety and skepticism. The creation of the PPS model was done with care and expertise. The organization contracted for this demonstration recruited 88 home health agencies, conducted interviews, extensive OASIS training, collected additional assessment data and reviewed in-home logs. The model was combined with claims data and then and only then did they conduct their analytic research. PPS was designed with stakeholders involvement. The contracted company worked side by side with home health clinical and operational staff, to better understand how their model would impact home health agencies. 

Will CMS please share the demonstration CMS used to develop the Home Health Grouping Model (HHGM)? 

HHGM is solely based on secondary Medicare and claims data. No interviews, no stakeholder involvement, no logs from patients home and no additional assessment data.

Are we (the Home Health industry) to understand one of the biggest changes to Medicare Perspective Payment System in 17 years is based on Medicare secondary and claims data and zero stakeholder involvement? 

As a matter of fact, no demonstration of any kind was used when CMS proposed their HHMG model. 

Understanding the importance of engaging providers, testing the model, solicit applications and securing participation, CMS as recent as 8/17/2017 changed it stance on CMS-5524P

Medicare Program; Cancellation of Advancing Care Coordination Through Episode Payment and Cardiac Rehabilitation Incentive Payment Models; Changes to Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement Payment Model (CMS-5524-P)

CMS: after careful review, we have determined that it is appropriate to propose to rescind the regulations at 42 CFR part 512, which relate to the EPMs and CR incentive payment model, and reduce the geographic scope of the CJR model for the following reasons."

CMS: "First, we believe that requiring hospitals to participate in additional episode payment models at this time is not in the best interest of the agency or the affected providers. Many providers are currently engaged in voluntary initiatives with CMS, and we expect to continue to offer opportunities for providers to participate in voluntary initiatives, including episode-based payment models. We are concerned that engaging in large mandatory episode payment model efforts at this time may impede our ability to engage providers, such as hospitals, in future voluntary efforts. 
In addition, if at a later date we decide to test these models, or similar models, on a voluntary basis, we would not expect to implement them through rulemaking, but rather would use methods of soliciting applications and securing participants' agreement to participate consistent with how we have implemented other voluntary models." 

CMS: "Finally, we believe that canceling the EPMs and CR incentive payment model, as well as altering the scope of the CJR model, offers CMS greater flexibility to design and test other episode-based payment models, while still allowing us to test and evaluate the impact of the ongoing CJR model on enhancing the quality of care while reducing costs.

If CMS is going to make such drastic reimbursement modifications to the home health industry, (which will have dire consequences), I feel it is only fitting CMS follow its standard practices and allow HHAs the same respect it extends to the hospital systems. Cancel this program and work with the home health industry to develop a model which make clinical, outcome and financial sense.

I think we should pay attention to historical ranges for all species. It is hard enough to make a living in agriculture as it is. We do not need additional hurdles that are not based on unified and sound judgement.

I am opposed to the attempt to allow the introduction of experimental populations outside of their historic range. This change would undermine the entire premise of the ESA's distinction between current and historical ranges for listed species. And it would create an unlimited ability for agencies to introduce species anywhere in the country without proper regard to historical evidence and ecological and biological science. It disregards the current and historical makeup of distinct ecosystems for purely political purposes.

The change would also clearly impact small entities like farms, ranches, and municipalities in the affected regions, something the notice fails to account for. While the change would not expand species protections, it would certainly broaden the geographic area in which current species protections may be applied and should, therefore, trigger a regulatory flexibility analysis. 

I urge you to rethink this proposal. While it may seem like a modest change, it is a massive change for the people and businesses impacted by their interaction with listed species.

I believe the 12.28 acres proposed to be designated for the Sonoyta mud turtles is necessary for the turtles to be free of nonnative predators and competitors. Currently, nonnative fish species such as tilapia and mosquitofish compete with the Sonoyta mud turtle for aquatic invertebrates. With the presence of these fish in the current habitat they might even reduce the population of the aquatic invertebrates that the turtles use as a food source. According to the Endangered Species Act of 1973, endangered species are allowed prohibitions with special regulation. The area designated to the turtles should be restrictive of any human interaction other than the administration to ensure there are are no adverse effects on the remaining population. In the meantime, the administration should find a way to increase the population by modifying the proposed area with necessities that ensure the turtles survival. The Sonoyta mud turtle lives within areas that commonly experience droughts and extreme heat, depleting the water needed for them to thrive. These waters provide the Sonoyta mud turtle food, prevent dryness, and give moisture to the soil the turtles use for nesting. The administration responsible for this should attempt to replicate the ideal environment for these turtles by supplying the habitat with water. This water can also create vegetation necessary to support the invertebrates that the turtles prey on and can also provide shelter from possible predators that the turtles may have when the population of turtles becomes stable enough as to not rely on the interference of humans to maintain their species.

Dear Food and Drug Administration,

I urge the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to promote Americans’ health by setting voluntary sodium reduction targets for processed, packaged, and prepared foods and beverages. 

Adult Americans are currently consuming about 50 percent more sodium than is recommended by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) and the Dietary Guidelines for Americans (DGA), among other health authorities – and most sodium consumption in the U.S. occurs through commercial food processing and preparation (including restaurants). Given the ubiquity of sodium in the food supply, consumers are limited in what they can do to protect themselves. But government-established voluntary targets can prompt industry to reformulate its products, reducing the toll of high blood pressure and heart disease. 

FDA took steps towards addressing this crisis in 2016 when it issued a draft guidance with both short- (2-year) and long-term (10-year) targets. The short-term targets have been finalized, but not the longer-term ones. Only FDA has the ability to encourage industry to act, and we urge it to do so by setting these targets as soon as possible.

Sincerely,
